claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical microstructure composed of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The starting alloy has limited room-temperature tensile ductility.
Dislocation pile-ups near internal phase boundaries cause the alloy's limited ductility and brittle failure.
A brief sub-eutectic annealing treatment can engineer beneficial interfacial structures without excessive coarsening.
The proposed heat treatment will redistribute alloying elements at the lamellar interfaces.
Element redistribution will form fine, coherent nanoscale secondary precipitates selectively along internal lamellar boundaries.
The boundary precipitates will improve interfacial bonding.
The boundary precipitates will act as effective dislocation sources and sinks.
The modified interfaces will permit more gradual accommodation of dislocation motion and reduce dislocation pile-ups.
Reducing dislocation pile-ups will lower local stress concentrations that otherwise trigger microcracking.
The treatment will improve room-temperature tensile ductility relative to the untreated alloy.
The treatment will maintain or slightly increase strength relative to the untreated alloy.
Mitigation of pile-ups and stress concentrations will reduce catastrophic failure.
The predicted benefits apply to room-temperature, quasi-static tensile loading.
Excessive treatment temperature or duration may cause microstructural coarsening or overaging.
Coarsening or overaging may eliminate the ductility improvement or reduce strength.
